title: Forty days
hook: Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, Jesus in the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clean Monday: a line of people asking pardon, and your line was forgive me.

A man alone on a mountain, with no bread and no water, while a cloud rests on the peak. Another, worn out and wanting to die, asleep under a juniper tree in the desert until someone wakes him and puts food beside his head. A third, just baptized, walking into the wilderness with nothing. Three stories from different parts of the Bible, and the same span of time turns up in all three. Not a week. Not a year. Long enough to hurt, and long enough to change you. Today, forty days.

Start with Moses. In Exodus he goes up to meet God and stays. The King James Bible says: "And he was there with the LORD forty days and forty nights; he did neither eat bread, nor drink water." He comes down carrying the words of the covenant on stone. Then Elijah. He has run for his life and lain down to die, and an angel brings him bread and water, twice. "And he arose, and did eat and drink, and went in the strength of that meat forty days and forty nights unto Horeb the mount of God." On that mountain he hears God not in the wind or the earthquake or the fire, but in a still small voice. And then Jesus. Matthew says: "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, he was afterward an hungred." The tempter comes, and Jesus answers him with words from scripture. Set the three side by side. Each is hard: hunger, exhaustion, testing. Each is spent close to God, away from the usual noise. And each one ends. Moses comes down. Elijah arrives. Jesus walks out to begin his work. The forty is not a life sentence; it's a passage with a far side. That's why churches link Lent to these stories, above all to Jesus in the desert: a season long enough for something to shift, and short enough to see the end of. This week ran from the waters of Theophany through prayer for unity, Brigid's rushes and Simeon's candle, to pancakes and a line of people saying forgive me. The last two stand at the very door of the forty days.

Let a few ideas come for one small thing you could keep for forty days: a walk each morning, a psalm a day, or giving up something that takes too much room. Pick one, not just the first, and picture day forty. If you pray, offer the forty days to God; if not, just hold the choice.
Forty days. The span of Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road, and Jesus in the desert. A hard passage, close to God, that comes to an end.
Your line: forty is enough. Every forty has a far side. Rest well.

howItsDone: During Lent, Christians often take on a practice for the season, such as fasting, giving something up, extra prayer, or giving to the poor, and churches connect the season to Jesus's forty days in the wilderness.

chat.says: Why is Lent forty days? Is it just a random number?
options: It echoes Moses, Elijah and Jesus: forty hard days close to God, that end.
It's the number of days Jesus spent in the tomb before Easter.
It's a round number for a long time, with no story behind it.
chat.meaning: Moses on the mountain, Elijah on the road and Jesus in the desert each spent forty days. Churches link Lent above all to Jesus's forty.

Elijah.meaning: a prophet of Israel who fled into the desert

Horeb.meaning: the mount of God, where Elijah heard a still small voice

covenant.meaning: God's binding promise with Israel, given through Moses

Lent.meaning: the season before Easter that churches link to these forties
